To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

activation of the parabracchial region of the mid-brain facilitates the response of geniculate relay neurons to certain visual stimuli, and that this facilitation can be explained by the disinhibition of local circuits within the lateral geniculata nucleus.

brain-stem activation facilitates visually evoked inhibition from the perigeniulate nucleus onto geniculate cells, and this effect is dependent on the spatial and temporal characteristics of the stimulus.
brain-stem stimulation enhances visual responses of cells in the perigeniculatet nucleus.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of cholinergic input to the thalamic reticular nucleus in the modulation of visual information processing in the thalamus.
the role played by brain-stem modulation of visual responses in the cat's lateral geniculate complex.

the role of the brain stem in modulating the activity of cells within the thalamus, in particular the lateral geniculatet nucleus (LGN), which is the main relay of visual information from the retina to the visual cortex.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the response properties of the majority of cells in the perigeniculat nucleus are modified by brain-stem stimulation.
the effect of brain stem activation on the visual responsiveness of perigeniculata cells is complex and variable.

activation of the parabracchial region of the pons has a complex, stimulus-specific effect on visual responses in the cat's geniculate complex, but that this effect is mediated through the perigeniculata.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the brain-stem cholinergic input to the thalamus is capable of enhancing the response of geniculate relay neurons, but the precise effect depends on the visual stimulus and the nature of the inhibitory circuitry that is being modulated.
the visual system is not simply a passive receiver of sensory information.

the brain-stem cholinergic input to the geniculate nucleus has a dual role: it facilitates transmission through the geniculate during arousal, while also enhancing the specificity of visual inputs to the geniculocortical system.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is a lot of plasticity in the visual system that we have yet to understand.
the visual responses of geniculate neurons can be modulated by brain-stem activation in a manner that depends on the spatio-temporal properties of the visual stimulus.
the response properties of geniculate relay neurons can be substantially altered during brain-stem activation.
